claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The proposed model integrates CALPHAD data and first-principles calculation data.
Training data will be drawn from high-entropy alloys similar to HfNbTiVAl10.
The hierarchical heterostructure and its multilevel chemical fluctuations influence the mechanical behavior of HfNbTiVAl10.
CALPHAD data capture thermodynamic stability relevant to the alloy's mechanical properties.
First-principles calculations describe electronic and atomic interactions relevant to the alloy's mechanical properties.
Combining CALPHAD and first-principles information in a machine-learning model will better represent the interactions governing Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
The hybrid model will improve prediction accuracy for mechanical properties by approximately 20–30% relative to single-fidelity methods.
The hybrid model will reduce computational demands by approximately 30–50% relative to single-fidelity methods.
Methods using CALPHAD or first-principles calculations independently are computationally intensive.
Methods using CALPHAD or first-principles calculations independently are less effective at predicting fracture-related properties.
The model may lose reliability for alloy compositions or microstructures that deviate substantially from its training data.
The model may lose reliability when processing conditions alter the hierarchical structure.
The proposed benchmark will compare blinded hybrid-model and baseline predictions against prospective tensile and fracture measurements on multiple HfNbTiVAl10 samples.
Benchmark measurements will include Young's modulus, offset yield strength, fracture toughness, and prediction computation time.

The hypothesis will be declared falsified if the model fails to improve prediction accuracy by at least 20% for at least two mechanical properties and also fails to reduce computational time by at least 30%.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome makes separate accuracy and efficiency claims, but the conjunctive falsification rule requires both an accuracy failure and an efficiency failure. Thus, failure of either central claim alone would not falsify the hypothesis.
